title: The Connection Approval Gap: Why a Completed Solar Job Isn't a Paid One Yet
excerpt: For solar and battery installers, panels going up isn't the end of the job. The final payment waits on a grid connection approval outside the installer's control, worth planning for as spring's pipeline grows.
content:
For a solar and battery installation business, the job looks finished the day the panels are up, the inverter is wired in, and the system switches on. Commercially, it often isn't. On most residential and small commercial contracts, the final payment milestone doesn't release until the distribution network service provider approves the new connection, and that approval sits entirely outside the installer's control.

Spring is when this gap bites hardest. Installation bookings lift across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria as households and small businesses get ahead of summer bills, and battery storage has become a bigger part of the average job, lifting the ticket size and the materials spend sitting out on each one. More jobs moving through the pipeline, each with more cash committed before the last payment lands, is a pattern worth planning for rather than discovering in a tight November.

None of this means anything has gone wrong. It is the normal shape of the industry's cash cycle. The problem is that most installers size their cash position around jobs completed, not around the lag between finishing the physical work and actually being paid for it.

Three Payments, One Long Wait

Most installation contracts are structured around a deposit, a progress payment and a completion payment, and each one sits at a different point in the job's actual cost curve. The deposit arrives before panels, inverters and mounting hardware are ordered, but rarely covers their full cost once battery storage is added to the job. Labour is committed, and often paid, well before the completion milestone is even invoiced. The final slice, frequently the largest single payment on the job, sits behind grid connection approval, and that approval can take anywhere from a few days to several weeks depending on the network operator and how busy the season is.

The installer has already paid for materials and labour on a job that, by every practical measure, is finished. The cash to cover that outlay is still sitting with the network operator's approval queue, not in the business's account.

Battery Attachment Changes the Shape of the Job

A straightforward panel installation and a panel-plus-battery installation are not the same cash commitment. Battery units carry a meaningfully higher unit cost than panels and inverters alone, and supplier terms on batteries do not always move in step with the rest of the materials order. Where a customer uses a finance provider to fund the battery component, the installer's payment timing depends on that third party's process as well as the network approval, adding a second variable to a cash cycle that already has one.

The result is that a growing attachment rate for battery storage, which is good for revenue and good for the customer relationship, also means more cash parked in a single job for longer, and a pipeline of twenty jobs awaiting connection approval carries a materially different cash exposure than it did when most of those jobs were panels alone.

What the Cash Position Should Actually Track

The useful number isn't total revenue booked for the month. It's how much cash is currently committed across every job sitting between completion and connection approval, set against what's actually due to suppliers, subcontractors and staff in the same window. Most job management systems already hold the data needed to build that view. Few installation businesses have turned it into a rolling cash picture rather than a job-by-job list.

A Working Capital Unlock does exactly this kind of mapping, tracing where cash is trapped between materials outlay, labour cost and the final payment milestone, and producing a prioritised view of where the gap can realistically be shortened, whether that's tightening deposit structure on battery-inclusive jobs or sequencing installs so connection approvals land in a steadier rhythm rather than all at once.

The other piece worth building before the pipeline grows further through summer is a weekly rather than monthly cash view, built around the business's actual payment milestones rather than a generic monthly report. That is the same discipline behind a weekly cash flow rhythm, applied to the specific shape of an installation calendar.

Spring's booking surge is good news for a solar and battery installer. What it quietly does to cash sitting between a finished roof and an approved connection is the part worth having mapped before summer's pipeline makes the gap harder to see, whether that pipeline is running through the Sunshine Coast or anywhere else along the East Coast.

faqs.q: Why does a finished solar installation sometimes take weeks to get paid?
faqs.a: The final payment milestone on most residential solar and battery contracts is tied to grid connection approval from the distribution network service provider, not to the physical completion of the install. That approval sits outside the installer's control and can take anywhere from a few days to several weeks, particularly during busier seasons when network operators are processing a higher volume of new connections.

faqs.q: What is a distribution network service provider and why does it matter for installers?
faqs.a: A distribution network service provider operates the local electricity network and must approve a new solar or battery connection before it can be switched on and the final payment invoiced. Approval timing varies by network and by season, and it is one of the few steps in an installation job that the installer genuinely cannot speed up through their own scheduling or staffing.

faqs.q: Does adding battery storage to a solar job change the cash flow risk for installers?
faqs.a: It usually does. Battery units carry a higher unit cost than panels and inverters alone, and finance arrangements on the battery component can introduce a separate payment timeline on top of the connection approval wait. A growing battery attachment rate is good for revenue, but it also means more cash sitting in each individual job for longer.

faqs.q: How many solar jobs in progress should concern an installer's cash position?
faqs.a: There is no fixed number, because it depends on how much materials and labour spend is actually sitting across jobs awaiting their final payment at any given time. The more useful exercise is mapping that exposure directly rather than estimating it, which is the starting point of a Working Capital Unlock.

faqs.q: Do Sunshine Coast and Gold Coast solar installers face different cash timing pressures?
faqs.a: The underlying pattern, materials and labour paid before connection approval clears, holds everywhere, but regions with high solar and battery uptake such as the Sunshine Coast can see network operators managing a larger volume of new connection requests at once, which may extend approval timing during the busiest parts of the season.

faqs.q: Would a weekly cash flow forecast help a growing solar and battery installation business?
faqs.a: For a business with jobs sitting at different stages between completion and connection approval, a weekly view catches timing pressure well before a monthly report would, especially once a dozen or more jobs are moving through the pipeline at once. A fractional CFO can build that rhythm around the business's actual payment milestones, deposit, progress, completion and connection, rather than a generic reporting calendar built for a different kind of business.

faqs.q: When should a solar installer get help setting up a proper cash flow view?
faqs.a: Before the spring and summer booking surge compounds the connection approval gap across a larger pipeline is the better time, rather than waiting until the cash position already feels tight. Mapping where cash is committed across the current job list takes far less time once it is done deliberately than once it has become a recurring source of stress each season. A discovery call is a reasonable place to start mapping it.
